This lesson covers a wide range of topics, which I will briefly outline. The main content includes writing engineering reports, creating and reviewing drawings, matters related to SPAC, as well as considerations for drawing review in North America. Additionally, we will briefly introduce matters pertaining to engineering budgets.

First, I will introduce the relevant aspects of engineering reports. As is well known, engineering reports are typically required to be written during the initial design phase, continuing through to the detailed design or engineering stage—specifically, the drawing production or SPAC (Specification and Code) preparation phase. For large-scale projects, report writing is essential, whereas smaller projects often proceed directly to the design phase. This is because large-scale projects involve tasks such as feasibility analysis and scheme evaluation.

In North America, projects under government or public sector jurisdiction usually require report submissions, even for smaller projects, as these reports are necessary for funding applications and project initiation. In contrast, small to medium-sized projects in the private sector generally do not require reports, though large-scale projects still need them. Whether for new construction or renovation projects, engineering reports are necessary, though their focus may differ.

The primary functions of engineering reports include analyzing current issues with facilities, buildings, or plants in existing projects, proposing multiple solutions, and evaluating the pros and cons, costs, and timelines of each option. The reports must also define the scope of work for each solution to assist clients in decision-making. Before project investment, clients need to assess factors such as project value, budget allocation, solution selection, and scheduling—engineering reports provide the analysis and decision-making support for this purpose.

Engineering reports serve to establish the design basis for subsequent design phases. Sometimes, reports must also be submitted as application documents to regulatory authorities. For example, in oil and gas projects in Alberta, Canada—where the province has abundant reserves but limited transportation capacity—large-scale projects like multi-billion-dollar pipeline constructions require approval from the National Energy Board and local government agencies.

The report must be submitted to the competent authority or local government for review and approval. Such reports are typically voluminous, with some even spanning over ten thousand pages, and the approval process may take up to a year and a half. These reports fall under the category of large-scale public sector projects.

Types of engineering reports include the following:

Types of engineering reports include the following:

Investment Analysis Report (IAR): Primarily for new projects, focusing on investment analysis, including cost estimation and evaluation of pros and cons.

Investigation Report (INR): Falls between investment and technical reports, mainly used for analyzing existing facilities.

Feasibility Study Report: Emphasizes technical feasibility analysis while also meeting financial requirements and budget constraints. Applicable to new or retrofit projects.

Basis of Design (BOD): Suitable for both new and retrofit projects. During the Schematic Design (SD) phase, design documents must be submitted alongside single-line diagrams and other drawings.

Basis of Design (BOD): Suitable for both new and retrofit projects. During the Schematic Design (SD) phase, design documents must be submitted alongside single-line diagrams and other drawings.

Front End Engineering Design (FEED): Primarily used for large-scale industrial projects such as oil, gas, mining, and power, typically involving investments in the billions. FEED is equivalent to the SD phase and requires the submission of extensive drawings and reports. For example, I once participated in a project for Statoil (Norwegian state oil company) where over 20 electrical engineers spent a year completing the FEED work, with a project investment of approximately 2 billion CAD.

Different project types and scales correspond to different report formats, with varying content and focus. FEED is primarily a technical report aimed at providing a basis for subsequent detailed design and preliminary design proposals.

For renovation projects, the first step is to conduct a site survey. The site conditions often stem from feedback or complaints from building occupants. When the property management or owners deem the issue beyond their capability to handle, they will engage a consulting firm and sign an agreement.

The consultant must conduct an on-site inspection to identify the problems and communicate with the client or operations management to clarify the project objectives and specific requirements, i.e., defining the project scope and needs. At the same time, relevant information and documents must be collected, and input from other disciplines and data are also crucial.

After gathering the necessary information, the on-site issues must be analyzed, technical documents reviewed, and relevant codes and standards consulted based on the site conditions, followed by necessary calculations. After comprehensively considering the client’s needs and on-site conditions, three options are typically proposed, detailing the scope of work, advantages and disadvantages, cost, and timeline for each, along with a recommended solution.

When proposing a solution, it is necessary to clarify its principles and rationale for recommendation. After completing the above tasks, the content should be compiled into a formal document, i.e., drafting a report.

When proposing a solution, it is necessary to clarify its principles and rationale for recommendation. After completing the above tasks, the content should be compiled into a formal document, i.e., drafting a report.

A report typically includes a cover page, and some reports require an engineer’s seal. The report content should consist of a table of contents, diagrams, photos, calculation data, and appendices, among other elements. As one of the key documents, the report must be reviewed by an internal senior engineer or lead engineer.

Depending on the project’s scale, complexity, and client requirements, a preliminary report is usually submitted first for client review and feedback. Upon receiving the feedback, the client’s comments must be incorporated into a revised version of the report, which is then resubmitted until final approval is obtained. This is the basic process for drafting an engineering report.

The previous discussion primarily focused on the renovation projects. For both renovation projects and new projects, the BOD report and SDR report generally place more emphasis on fundamental content. In fact, there is little difference between the BOD report and the SDR report—the former is similar to a conceptual design report, while the latter resembles a schematic design report.

The processes are largely similar, but for renovation projects, additional steps such as site surveys and client information collection are required. The differences in other aspects are minor and will not be elaborated further. Below is a brief overview of the key points for drafting these reports.

For Chinese individuals, writing reports does pose certain difficulties, with the main obstacle being insufficient English writing skills. While listening, speaking, and reading abilities in English may be passable, writing—especially composing well-structured and logically rigorous reports—remains a significant challenge.

The first issue is how to balance design budget with design depth and quality. Overseas, design work is typically divided into phases. For instance, if a project only progresses to the preliminary design stage, there’s no need to delve into subsequent work to avoid resource wastage in case of project cancellation. This is particularly evident in the design industry, especially among private design firms and large enterprises, which enforce strict budget controls. Time costs are acutely reflected in the design sector, as designers are billed by the hour—additional work hours directly translate to extra expenses. Therefore, design depth should align with the project phase, delivering only the necessary technical documentation for that stage.

Secondly, building projects (e.g., offices, schools, government buildings—commercial projects) and industrial projects (e.g., oil fields, mines, power facilities) operate under fundamentally different models. In commercial projects, consulting is usually independent, whereas in industrial projects, consulting and construction are often bundled under EPC (Engineering, Procurement, and Construction) contracts. Additionally, their design budgets differ significantly. Commercial project designs tend to be more schematic with limited budgets, while industrial project designs are highly detailed, with every aspect meticulously considered due to their ample design budgets. For example, in an industrial project, designing a switchgear might allocate 40 hours of work, covering all technical issues and coordination to produce a comprehensive material requisition. In contrast, commercial projects typically simplify this step to drafting specifications before direct procurement.

Industrial project consultants provide exhaustive equipment specifications because they have abundant time. For instance, I once worked on a generator project for an oil company where the generator itself cost $150,000, yet the design fees reached $200,000—highlighting the emphasis on design depth in industrial projects.

When executing projects in the commercial sector, costs may range between $20,000 to $40,000, but actual variations can span 5 to 10 times. There is also a notable disparity in design depth between North America and China. Chinese design drawings typically achieve about 66% to 70% of the depth seen in North America, primarily due to faster project timelines, tighter schedules, and lower budgets domestically. Additionally, domestic contractors often possess higher skill levels, with design institutes providing only conceptual plans, leaving detailed implementation to on-site resolution.

The difference between BOD and Spec isn’t particularly significant—the main distinction lies in the level of detail.

BOD is merely a design scheme, design method, or design guideline—it serves as the foundation for design. On the other hand, specifications (spec) are extremely detailed, hence referred to as “bookspec.”

For instance, in conventional construction projects, a complete bookspec can span hundreds or even thousands of pages. In contrast, a BOD typically requires only around twenty pages, offering a more generalized overview as a design directive—essentially a written finalization. Specifications, however, lay out highly granular requirements for specific products.

Therefore, it is advisable to include a clause in the drawings or general specifications explicitly stating that the most stringent requirement shall apply in case of deviations. This can be clearly stipulated in the contract to avoid disputes.

In other words, unless specifically stipulated that drawings take precedence, when there is ambiguity between the specifications and drawings regarding the definition of the same technical parameter, the more stringent standard shall be applied. This not only safeguards the interests of the owner but also prevents contractors from adopting the minimum standard to save costs.

First is internal review, which mainly refers to reviews within the discipline. After designers complete drawings or other design documents, they need to submit them to senior engineers, chief engineers, or lead engineers for review or approval.

Internal review refers to evaluations conducted within a specific discipline. After designers complete drawings or other design documents, they must submit them to senior engineers, chief engineers, or lead engineers for review or approval.

Squad check, known domestically as drawing co-signing, involves joint verification across disciplines to ensure proper coordination. For example, the electrical discipline may require exhaust fans or air conditioning cooling systems in the transformer room (electro room), and the mechanical discipline must verify whether these are reflected in the drawings. Simultaneously, the mechanical discipline confirms whether air handling units and water pumps are properly supplied with power. The electrical discipline must also coordinate with architects on equipment box installation locations, including details such as transformer rooms requiring double doors instead of single doors.
